title: OpenEvidence raises $250M Series D at a $15B valuation with a16z and hospital-system LPs
subtitle: The clinical-search platform used by roughly 40% of US physicians now trades at nearly double its January mark, and hospital systems joined the cap table directly.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenEvidence has raised $250 million in a Series D round at a $15 billion post-money valuation, according to reporting on September 25. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with undisclosed hospital systems participating directly on the cap table. The mark is roughly 25% higher than the $12 billion valuation the company hit in January, and about 55% higher than the $9.71 billion figure that surfaced from an earlier late-stage round led by a16z and Byers Capital. Company disclosures put physician usage at around 40% of US doctors and describe rapid growth in decision-support and drug-development-adjacent workflows.

The interesting signal here is not the raise. It is who joined the round. Hospital systems taking direct equity in a clinical-AI vendor is a departure from the standard hospital-vendor relationship, where systems buy on multi-year contracts and negotiate down. Equity aligns them the other direction: the model that gets deployed better is also the one that pays out. That pattern, if it holds, could reshape how clinical AI is priced — moving away from per-seat SaaS and toward outcomes-linked revenue with strategic-investor hospitals as reference customers. Abridge's $775 million enterprise deal with the US Department of Veterans Affairs, announced days earlier, points at the same shift from a different angle.

OpenEvidence sits in a category that grew out of Google-for-doctors and is now trying to become the reasoning layer above the EHR. That is a bigger and messier prize. It requires the search product to be right about drug interactions, contraindications, and workup pathways — not just to return plausible-looking citations — and to keep being right as the underlying medical literature moves. The category's incumbents (UpToDate, DynaMed) have accuracy but not the modeling stack; the new entrants (OpenEvidence, Glass, Hippocratic-tier clinical LMs) have the stack but are still building the accuracy story. A $15 billion mark is the market betting that the second gap closes faster than the first.

Takeaway for learners: healthcare AI's evaluation regime is more like a regulated industry than like a consumer product, and the metrics that matter are the ones a medical board or a plaintiff's attorney would ask about. If you want to work here, learn the difference between a clinical-decision-support system, a clinical-search tool, and a device — the FDA draws hard lines between them, and where a product lands on that spectrum determines what it can say, what it must prove, and who is on the hook when it is wrong.
